questions.question: What motivated you to go on exchange? (pick the most important one) *
questions.answer: Explore new cultures

questions.question: Which aspects were crucial to choosing your study destination? *
questions.answer: The aspects that were crucial to choosing my study destination were that it was English-speaking, that previous students' experiences had been great, and that the course catalogue had a lot of classes that I thought looked super interesting.

questions.question: How would you rate your overall study abroad experience? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: Absolutely a 10. Honestly, the reason why I haven't gotten around to writing this review before now is because I simply don't know how to describe how fantastic my experience was! I hadn't even been in Toronto Union Station for 2 full minutes the day I first arrived looking for a train to take to the university, when I had already made two new friends from Israel. They were also going to be exchange students at Western, and even living in the same building as me! I enjoyed every minute I had with all the amazing people I met from ALL around the world! I remember when I first arrived in the suite late at night the 31st of August, I was unlocking the door to my room when all of a sudden two of my suitemates stuck their heads out from each of their doors, and it was at that exact moment,  that I just knew that it was going to be the best. semester. ever. Since that day, we've been pretty much inseparable. I knew it all along, but especially the very last morning when everyone woke up at 5 AM to wave goodbye to me and I got on the bus, it hit me that I had truly made these friends for life. And guess what?! Not one day has gone by since I left Canada that I haven't talked to them in some way or another, whether that's by audio on the phone, sending pictures or funny jokes, snaps, or whatever it is!

questions.question: How easy was it to find the information you needed to know upon arrival? *
questions.answer: Super easy! Western was really good about emailing us updates of what we needed to keep an eye out for, so I just booked a ticket to Toronto and figured that I would figure it out along the way, which I did! Everything is in English and most of the time French too, so it wasn't hard at all.

questions.question: What assistance, if any, did you receive when you arrived at your study destination? *
questions.answer: Once I arrived at Western and “checked in” there was a free taxi that took the friends that I had just made and I to Alumni House where we were going to be living, and a goodie bag with snacks and all the information we needed for the orientation events the next day. The university was also really good at hosting a plethora of activities that really allowed you to get to know the others who were there. In addition, everyone is assigned a soph, both relating to an individuals' housing and also for their faculty, which act as an older brother or sister and give tours, showed us around, and really helped us feel welcome and at home.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the orientation and assistance available to students at your host institution upon arrival? *
Additional comments
questions.answer: I highly recommend participating in O Week. It might be an expensive wristband, but it was so worth it in the way that it really allowed me the opportunity to bond and make a ton of new friends already in the first week of being there. Other than that, the counselors and advisors at the (IGAB) international and graduate affairs building were super helpful in answering any questions one might have.

questions.question: How did you find housing? *
questions.answer: I found housing through my host institution

questions.question: Did you live on campus or off campus? *
questions.answer: On campus

questions.question: What options were available for on campus housing? *
questions.answer: I think the vast majority of students living on campus lived in the same residence: Alumni House. I think if you wanted to live in another house, you had to request it.

questions.question: What options were available for meal plans or cooking facilities? *
questions.answer: You could either opt into the meal plan OR choose to be in charge of your own food. The suites in Alumni House each have their own kitchen, but you'll be in charge of getting the general kitchen supplies. My suitemates and I got most of the stuff we needed from dollarama where you can get a pan, utensils, etc and other essentials for super cheap.

questions.question: What should future exchange students know about living in on campus housing? *
questions.answer: We never had any problems with this, but it can be helpful to make a chart to keep track of expenses such as soap, toilet paper, etc and just add it up/reimburse in the end.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the housing available to students? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: If you have the option to live on campus, I would highly, highly recommend it!!! I loved it! The majority of exchange and international students lived in Alumni House, which was divided into 3 wings, east, central, and west. The living arrangements were perfect, just enough privacy with your own room with a bed and desk, but a shared kitchen, living room, and bathroom with your 3 other suitemates so you could cook and eat breakfast together, or have movie nights, but at the same time be able to close the door and work on school work when needed. It felt JUST right. And it was also SUPER nice that all of the exchange students lived in the same building (Alumni House), because it provided an optimal opportunity to get to meet other people who were in the same boat as you.

questions.question: How easy did you find the registration process at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: Registering for classes and applying for housing was super straightforward.

questions.question: Please describe the registration process at your host institution *
questions.answer: I think that we were just sent links to online course picker and the course catalogue, where the course descriptions and prerequisites were listed. If I remember correctly, we were able to add course titles on a list (requested), they were then sent to the appropriate department (pending), and then once they were approved, it was added to your course schedule (enrolled), and you could therefore see the status of each class. If you don't meet the prerequisites, and are denied a course, don't worry, you can just request another! Don't hesitate to contact the student center and ask for help, I did that, and was even able to sign up for a second-year French course (even though I study molecular biomedicine) by showing them documentation of having studied sufficient French in high school and taking a quick placement test.

questions.question: What kind of help was available? *
questions.answer: Please read my description of the registration process above.

questions.question: How successful were you in registering for the classes you wanted? *
questions.answer: I was extremely successful in registering for just the classes that I wanted. I even got to enroll in a French translation course last minute as an elective!

questions.question: What advice would you offer to future exchange students about registration at your host institution? *
questions.answer: Just remember to check that courses that you are interested in are being offered on the main Western campus, not King's, Huron, or Brescia.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the academic programme at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: The educational aspect was phenomenal, and my professors were absolutely great. Even though the class sizes are small in Copenhagen, quite frankly, I'm not sure any of my professors that I have had have ever known my name. In Canada, even in the classes that had over 200 students, the professors really made an effort to establish a connection with the students and many knew my name and my strengths and weaknesses in the class.

questions.question: Were you a BA or MA student at UCPH when you were on exchange? *
questions.answer: BA

questions.question: Please elaborate on the level of courses *
questions.answer: If you are going on exchange in the first half year of your third year studying in Copenhagen, I would recommend taking courses in the 2000-4000 level. The level of courses that I took when I was there were a French translation course and an Immunology (only lecture) course at the 2000 level, a Genetics course at the 3000 level, and a Neuroscience (essay) course at the 4000 level.

questions.question: How did the style of teaching at your host institution compare with that of UCPH? *
questions.answer:
It was very different. In Copenhagen, other than a few mandatory labs, the only thing that counts for your grade is the final exam. At Western, it was much more like the American/Canadian system where you have a lot of homework due and have a lot of projects to turn in and quizzes/tests to take throughout the semester which make up about 70% of your final grade, whereas the final exam only makes up the remaining 30% or so. Personally, I prefer that much better, since it helps me stay on track and I also have a better idea of what I am expected to know for the final exam. Not only that, but you work hard for your grade the whole term and know that with the final exam, depending on how much you prepare, you can pretty much only drop one letter grade or increase it by one letter grade.
Note that Western's grading scale might be different than you expect: 
A+ = 90-100 
A = 80-90
B = 70-80
C = 60-70
D = 50-60
F = 50 or below

questions.question: How long were you on exchange? *
questions.answer: 1 semester

questions.question: Please list the courses you were enrolled in during your first semester. *
questions.answer:
Anatomy and Cell Biology 4451 F/G Integrative Neuroscience
French 2305 A/B Translation: Comparative Stylistics
Microbiology and Immunology 2500 A/B Biology of Infection and Immunity
Biology 3592 A/B Principles of Human Genetics

questions.question: What specific courses would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer: I would recommend taking ANY of the courses that I took (listed above). Each was super interesting in its own unique way and had a different learning structure/strategy for how the class was run. In French class we would get a few exercises from a little book from the 1960's assigned to have done by the next class. In the Genetics course, we had a big case study project where we had to pretend to be genetic counselors and “teach” various concepts to the patient and their family, we also had a forum where we would read papers and post questions open-ended questions/respond to others' questions, a bioethics team-debate and reading logs. In Neuroscience we had weekly written assignments and one really big presentation, and finally, the Immunology course was just lectures and grading based on the midterms. It was refreshing that they were all set up differently!

What unexpected costs did you encounter? *
questions.answer: I didn't really have any unexpected costs.

questions.question: What items were more or less expensive than you expected? *
questions.answer: All of the items were about the same price that I had expected.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the non-academic opportunities (clubs, sports, etc.) at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: Attend as many events as you can and try your best to get involved to get yourself a community, because that's the best way to make friends and feel a part of the school!

questions.question: What kinds of cultural, athletic and social activities were available for students at your host institution? *
questions.answer: There was homecoming, intramural sports, house-related craft events like door-decorating, movie nights, and cultural events like global cafe each Thursday that focused on cuisine and traditions from a different country around the world each week.

questions.question: Which non -academic activities would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer: Some of my friends/roomies and I would go to the recreation center in the morning, either to use the bike machines or go to the pool. It's so well-equipped and the pool is huge. You can also go for a walk in one of the nearby local parks. I was there during autumn and it was SO BEAUTIFUL when the leaves started to turn red orange and yellow and fell from the trees. In late October, one day we went to Ross Park (only a five minutes walk away from Western) and we took the most INCREDIBLE photos in heaps of bright orange leaves!!! You might also want to go to an Apple farm or a Pumpkin patch, the nature is wonderful! Lastly, in December, my roommate found out Mariah Carey was having a Christmas concert in the Scotiabank Arena in Toronto, so we went and it was THE. BEST. EXPERIENCE. EVER! If you can find things to do like that, you'll make some great memories! Towards the end, the World cup in soccer was also playing on screen at the Spoke (the student restaurant/bar), so it was really exciting for me to go see it with my French friends when France was playing.

questions.question: What do you recommend other visiting students see or do on their weekends or holidays? *
questions.answer:
I highly recommend visiting Toronto and Niagara Falls on a weekend or holiday. For Toronto, you can book a bus on Megabus that departs at 6 AM right outside Elgin Hall and drives directly to Toronto in a little over 2 hours, and you can take the same bus back in the evening for only about $25 dollars each way. When I came I took the train, which is also do-able, it's just more expensive and takes a long time, so if you can, you should go by bus.
You can also travel by plane during reading week, that way you have more time to explore another place in Canada and have more than just a three day weekend/thanksgiving off and can go somewhere farther.

questions.question: How easy was it to adjust to the local culture of your exchange site? *
questions.answer: For me, I found it super easy to “assimilate” when I came to London and also in adjusting to the school system, as that was what I had once been used to having grown up in the US. Of course, I can't say for sure that this wasn't special in my case, because London is in fact apparently very similar to the American model, but it really seems as if the other exchange students that I lived with (and some of whom are still there), are having a blast! Everyone that I have talked to who went to Western all said that they had a fantastic experience there, so I really think that Western just has a really good exchange program and is very open and welcoming. I know for my part at least, I was really lucky in that everyone I met was super nice and friendly, and that it wasn't hard to adjust to at all!

questions.question: Do you have any tips for socializing with local students?
questions.answer: Don't be afraid to introduce yourself and talk to people in your classes, everyone is super nice! It's also a good idea to form/join a study group with Canadian students from your classes even if it is just with one other person and meeting at the library or something. Everyone is super down-to-earth.

questions.question: What, if any, cultural differences did you find particularly challenging? *
questions.answer: Luckily I didn't find any cultural differences there challenging!

questions.question: What parts of the culture did you most appreciate? *
questions.answer: This might not fall under the culture aspect, but I really like how, by living on campus, especially with the “old fashioned” buildings it really felt like a boarding school setting, which I thought was really nice when everyone was so kind there, so you were living with your best friends! Also the fact that strangers aren't afraid to talk to you was very refreshing! Once, my suitemate and I took the bus to go to the farmer's market and a elderly Canadian woman in the bus started talking to us and asking us how we liked Western and gave us recommendations about what to try from the farmer's market. I remember her mentioning “the cherry fritters.” Then, by coincidence the next Friday morning the following week, the same woman happened to be on the bus and we could recognize her and again we talked on the way there. A real Canadian local! How fun!

questions.question: What are the three most important things you would tell a UCPH student who is going to your host institution on exchange? *
questions.answer:
I would tell a fellow student who is coming to Western to 1. Keep an open mind; I really had no idea what to expect when I came, but I had an open-minded mindset and was ready to try living in a new place, thrive with learning, and meet a bunch of amazing people!
2. Don't overpack, you will thank me later. Especially books, they are so heavy and a hassle!
3. If you have the chance, write someone a card, maybe to someone in your family or an old friend, it's so nice to have a homemade postcard with an envelope with your Canadian address on it, a Canadian stamp, and it'll bring back so many good memories! Plus, they might even send one back to you! ;)
4. If you are going in the fall, collect some orange leaves right after they have fallen from the trees and press them in a book for about a week or so and they'll be perfect, you can even make a garland out of them! I still have mine in a box as a souvenir and I love it!

questions.question: Is there any other information that you think might prove useful to future exchange students attending your host institution? *
questions.answer: Nothing that I can think of!

questions.question: What was the most rewarding part of your exchange experience? *
questions.answer: The most rewarding part of my exchange experience was the friends I made. I still talk to my friends I met in Canada every single day. In January I even went to Lyon to visit one of the friends I made after she had returned to France from London. How cool is that!

questions.question: What was the greatest challenge during the exchange? *
questions.answer: It might sound hard to believe but I really believe my exchange was the most perfect exchange that I could ever wish for! I really didn't find anything challenging while there. The only thing, which is not even a big deal or anything, was that the vacuum never really worked, and it didn't matter which one you tried; but honestly, I'm happy it didn't because you should know how many laughs we've had lugging that thing around and “complaining” to the front desk time after time and them promising a new one by the end of the semester, and people returning each “new” one (even though they weren't new at all) after accidentally cutting over the wire and returning it, bahaha! It's kind of one of those, “if you know, you know” moments! So even that, I wouldn't change!

questions.question: Any other comments?
questions.answer: If you come to Western I hope you have as much of a blast as I did!!!! :)

questions.question: Do you agree to share your travel report with other fellow students? *
questions.answer: Yes
